lesson.title: Protocols That Remember What Happened Before
lesson.summary: A stateful protocol keeps track of context across a sequence of messages so that later exchanges depend on earlier ones, which is what connection oriented protocols like TCP require to function and what distinguishes protocols like FTP from simpler, memoryless request response exchanges.
lesson.body:
A stateful protocol is one in which the meaning or handling of a given message depends on what has already happened earlier in the exchange, which requires both sides to keep track of context, or state, across multiple messages rather than treating each one as an isolated, self-contained event. This is a direct consequence of connection oriented service: establishing a connection, as TCP does with its handshake, only makes sense if both endpoints then remember that the connection exists and track its progress, which is exactly what makes TCP a stateful protocol rather than a simple message passing scheme.

TCP's statefulness is formalized as an actual state machine. A TCP connection at any point in time is in one of a defined set of states, including CLOSED before anything has happened, SYN SENT and SYN RECEIVED during the handshake, ESTABLISHED once the connection is fully open and data can flow, and several states like FIN WAIT and TIME WAIT during an orderly shutdown. Both endpoints track which state the connection is currently in, along with sequence numbers, acknowledgment numbers, and window sizes, and this tracked state is exactly what lets TCP reject a stray segment that does not belong to any connection it currently recognizes, since a segment arriving without a matching, established connection state simply does not fit anywhere and gets rejected.

FTP, the file transfer protocol, is a useful application layer example of statefulness that is easy to reason about concretely. A client connects to an FTP server and authenticates once using USER and PASS commands. After that, the server remembers the authenticated session and tracks additional context such as the client's current working directory. Subsequent commands like LIST, to view files, or RETR, to download a file, are interpreted in light of that remembered context, so the client does not need to resend credentials or a full path with every single command. Contrast this with a stateless exchange, where each request would need to carry everything necessary to understand it on its own, since nothing from a previous message is remembered.

Statefulness is not free, and the tradeoff is worth naming directly. Maintaining state means an endpoint must allocate memory for every active connection or session, which limits how many concurrent connections a server can realistically track, and it creates a fragility that a purely stateless design does not have: if that state is lost, for example a firewall or load balancer that tracks connections restarts and forgets everything it knew, the two original endpoints may still believe their connection is alive even though the middlebox no longer has any record of it, leading to a connection that appears to hang with no clear signal to either side about what went wrong.

This tradeoff is exactly why some protocols are deliberately designed to be stateless even when they run over a stateful transport connection, and why systems that need to scale to very large numbers of clients often go out of their way to minimize how much state any single component has to remember. Recognizing whether a protocol is stateful or stateless is one of the most practical questions to ask about any new protocol, because it predicts both what that protocol can guarantee and exactly how it will fail when something in the middle of the path forgets what it was supposed to remember.
